utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, for the Prosecution I'm Tom Hannis, along with Gerard Dobbyn and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are no preliminary matters, may the usher -- would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, good morning to you. Before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- counsel for Mr. Stanisic begins his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will start my examination proceeding from your answer to my learned friend Mr. Krgovic's question which is at page 24842 of yesterday's transcript. Mr. Krgovic asked you about the difficulties you had in receiving and transmitting dispatches in the period you discussed yesterday, and I will read just a part of your answer from the transcript. [As read] "For instance, there is one dispatch that I saw, it was shown to me by the gentleman from the Prosecution when I was giving them my statement. My signature can be found on that dispatch?" And you go on to say the dispatch speaks of the scope of what I'm discussing now and it would be the best illustration of what I'm saying. Do you recall what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So do you recall that this is precisely what you told colleague Krgovic yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll show you the dispatch. It's an exhibit. It's P668. I need page 1 in both versions. Yes. That's what we need. Mr. Jankovic, let me ask you first, is this the dispatch you were discussing yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the one I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please pause before answering.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the dispatch I had in mind. Yes. It is a good copy. You can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I have a hard copy if you want to have it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please, it would be much easier. If you don't mind. It is a bit tiring to read from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I would like to clarify a point from this dispatch. So is this the dispatch, please confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this is the dispatch shown to you by the Prosecution during the interview; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's where I remember it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Tell us, we have a signature in handwriting. Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my abbreviated signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, there is a note on the dispatch indicating that it was impossible to transmit it to the first two addresses, i.e., the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And there's a bracket there and one Goran signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is my question: Were these precisely the difficulties that you were referring to, namely, in this case, you weren't able to transmit dispatches to the MUP at Pale and the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely why I cited this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. You no longer need to look at the dispatch because I will be putting questions of a general nature to you now.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just add something? The reason, in fact, why I referred to the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'll ask you about it in some of my questions. But -- right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be as brief as possible. The contents don't matter. I will not be talking about them. I saw the dispatch for the first time when it was shown to me by a gentleman from the Prosecution, otherwise I would have long forgotten about it. It speaks very clearly to the issues we were discussing, namely, the quality of the communication links, et cetera. Look at what it says at the top "dx open" and then circled and then a "sh" is added and then my signature. "Open" or "sh" stands for the status of confidentiality of the document and it would normally be indicated by the author of the document. Apparently the author of this particular document - and it is Simo Drljaca who signed - wasn't so privy to these rules and didn't put it properly. And then the operator who transmits dispatches and makes corrections where they are needed in this case contacted me and ask that the designation of confidentiality be changed, in other words, that it not be an open dispatch but that it be coded and that's why I made the correction that you can see here. There are three addresses to which the dispatch is supposed to be transmitted, namely, the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Army of Republika Srpska, and the CSB in Banja Luka. The communications operator, one Goran, indicated that we were unable to send the dispatch to the two first addresses. Now, the CSB which was closest to us in terms of communication links was reached and the dispatch was sent. The handwritten note contains a date, the 18th, or rather, 1840 Rodic and then the 3rd of August at 10.00 Milan. It was standard procedure that dispatches designated as "dx" would be sent no later than within two hours, whereas in reality they would be sent right away. However, this dispatch indicates that the dispatch was sent two days later, which indicates the length of time that the dispatches had to be delayed before they were sent and in certain circumstances it really defeated the purpose of the dispatches to begin with, but that was the circumstance prevailing at the time. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And at times you, or rather, you've just anticipated my next question. The teleprinter system, the telex system with the various coding and confidentiality designations constitute the basis of the workings and the running of the Ministry of the Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, it was precisely that system which failed to operate for most of 1992 and in most of the areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, even locally; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I cannot speak in greater detail about the links outside of the routes between Prijedor, Banja Luka, and Sarajevo. I wouldn't be able to speak about them with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back to your yesterday's evidence. You spoke of your deployment to the front line as part of that unit. Do you recall talking about it as part of that police unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In that role of yours, you also dealt with communications; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, solely with communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But at the time what you were doing had a military purpose, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way this combat unit was organised was that it was part of a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me follow-up this answer of yours with this question. Members of the Prijedor public security station would, as part of these military purposes, be deployed to other front lines, not just this one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On occasions such as these, would they be part of the communications system of the public security station in Prijedor, i.e., would they have been in communication with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will show you two more documents now to support some of your answers of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call-up 65 ter 616D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, if you need a hard copy for your easier perusal --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's all right. I can read it off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read it to yourself and then I'll put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a short document.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, yesterday you said that, locally, members of the public security station would receive their salaries and the equipment they needed from the local level; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this document confirms it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We can tell that the document is of the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long this situation prevailed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Not just a couple of days. At least the entire summer, perhaps through to the end of the year. Anyway, throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise the signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And can you read the signature block?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says Milomir Stakic, president of the municipality, but I don't recognise his signature. I don't know if it's his.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But in general, were you aware that Simo Drljaca, Ranko Travar dealt with salaries, uniforms, and everything else in co-operation with the Crisis Staff. Were you aware of this? You did speak about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you all of us worried about whether we would be paid our salaries and we would talk about it amongst ourselves that the municipality had set aside funds for this purpose, that a salary would be forthcoming, et cetera. As for uniforms, there were uniforms that were procured, but I don't know who paid for them. I can only assume that they came from that quarter, whereas I am certain that this was the case with salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know how come this document hasn't been admitted yet and I don't see any other way of admitting it than through this witness. The witness spoke in great detail yesterday about payments and the supply of uniforms. So I do believe that we have passed the threshold required for the admission of a document. I think it is helpful for the case in general and it's helpful for some of the submissions that the Defence will be putting in our final brief. So I please -- I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection or two. The fact that may be helpful to Defence submissions is not a reason for admitting it. The witness says it says Stakic but he doesn't recognise his signature. At most it says there was a conclusion that Mr. Drljaca and two others were charged with making a comprehensive review of the possibilities but there's no indication from this witness or any other evidence so far that a review was done or what happened. So I don't know what it adds to the witness's testimony at this point and he is not able to establish the foundation for the authenticity of this document. And it has limited relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, do you have a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness described how things worked in practice and this document confirms it quite clearly. There's not a shred of doubt about the authenticity of this document, contrary to what the Prosecution are saying. This is an official document received from the Prosecution. It is not a Defence exhibit. I mean, we are tendering it but we received it from the Prosecution. There are no doubts about its authenticity, and as for the contents, well, the witness did speak about that. So I believe that's the foundation for the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I say a word or two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would prefer you to -- not to volunteer evidence. If counsel has a supplemental question, he may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D813, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I'll show you another document which is an exhibit. We will have no difficulty there. It's P803.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance to give the document to the witness. It may be easier for him to read this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read it to yourself and then I'll put my question to you. I'll give you three to four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Jankovic, did you know that there was a special unit in town, an intervention platoon of this kind, as it says in the document? Did you have the opportunity to see these people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall seeing anything of the kind that is described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, it states here that this was formed by the Crisis Staff. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. This is at another level that has nothing to do with me, so I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So my question has to do with your work. This, or an intervention unit of this kind, was it in the communications system of the public security station and did it have anything to do with you and did you provide communication means?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was an intervention platoon that was called that way in unofficial talk, and I can see here that it refers to personnel from existing police forces. Carry out from the existing police forces. But I didn't know anybody from that so-called intervention platoon. I knew them but outside of the service that Zigic, he was there but he was never in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said from the military and the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, paragraph 2, that's what it says, from the police and the army. I didn't know those people. They were not from the police thus.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the essence is that they were not from the police and they were not in your police system of communication, yes or no, I mean answer please whether they were in your system?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite clear, they were not in our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, Mr. Jankovic, now when we look at this order together from which we can see that the Crisis Staff is forming some sort of special unit over there that had nothing to do with the public security station, and we can see that salaries for the police were being -- and for uniforms were being provided at the local level. It seems then that Prijedor - when I say "Prijedor," I mean the Prijedor authorities - was quite independent in relation to the rest of Republika Srpska. Do you share this view?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is a little bit unclear to me, but as far as I understand I can just repeat what I said yesterday. Simo didn't really pay much attention to these others except for those that had brought him there and that's the municipal authorities. I'm sorry, I apologise --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you directly. From these documents that I have showed you -- I apologise. Or actually, I want to clarify my question. When you actually say that he didn't pay too much attention to others, are you thinking of Pale, for example, or Banja Luka and that he actually -- actually, he did these people at the local level more -- well --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that he was going by his own mind. If he needed to co-operate with somebody, then he would go to the municipality. I don't know who he talked to, who was issuing what sort of assignments to whom, that is something that I don't know. But I do know that what was earlier was disrupted. The relationships were regular. Before the chief of the police would go to Banja Luka and Sarajevo. He would also go to the Komitet as well. But this one, he mostly went there across the road to that municipality. When I say "municipality," I would just like to make sure that we're not talking about the municipality, we're talking about the building. Where he went, I don't know whether he went to the municipal authorities, to the SDS, to the board, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you mean he went to Banja Luka and Sarajevo. When you said that you're thinking about the pre-war period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the pre-war period up until the multi-party elections -- well, not Simo but whoever was at that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So it was like that until Simo Drljaca came and then it changed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then it came back after that, but 1992 was turbulent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So when you're talking about this disruption in relations, you're talking about 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1992. I -- I would just like for the sake of caution. I couldn't say that in 1992 he didn't go to Banja Luka. I don't know. Perhaps he did, but I'm not aware that he ever went to Pale. Perhaps he did but I don't know that, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Jankovic, I don't have any further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I will have a lot of questions for you. I would ask that -- well, first of all, let me ask you: Do you understand English? Do you read or understand English?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. English texts that have to do with electronics or technical texts, yes, that I can use. But as for the rest, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I ask was that it seemed at times you were looking at the transcript and you were able to follow somewhat in English where we were. That's why I asked the question. I would ask that you do try and watch the transcript and see when the typing stops before you begin your answers to my questions. That will make it easier for the interpreters to keep up with you because you're a pretty fast talker.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, that is why I am looking at the transcript, so that when it stops I can continue. This is why I was looking at it, not in order to translate. And I don't actually understand it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I just want to ask you a few questions about your background. I understand you started working in the police in 1980 and you retired in 2008; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from late June 2008, in late June 2008, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when were you first appointed to the position of chief of the communications and cryptographic data protection section or department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 15th or the 20th of August, five days here or there, so August 1980. 1980. It was definitely mid-August, I think it was the 15th, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you started out as the chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that the position you held throughout your entire career, until your retirement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the official names for that post changed, but the description of duties was always the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then, as I recall, you moved to Banja Luka in 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st of November, yes, yes, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you worked as the chief in Banja Luka from 2001 until your retirement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I wasn't chief of the department, but I was chief of a sector, technical maintenance, whereas in Prijedor I was in charge of maintenance and utilisation because the station was smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. I think you told us that your wife worked at Prijedor SJB in 1992 as -- in the economic or white collar crime section; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did she work there throughout 1992, the whole year?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is her name Miroslava? I've seen that on a payroll document I think.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslavka, Miroslavka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll have to help me with my Serbian pronunciation sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us before that there was a Dusan Jankovic who was the commander of the police at Prijedor during at least part of 1992. Are you and he related in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He is from Kozara and I'm from Eastern Bosnia from near Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go into private session? I have a couple of questions that I want to ask that relate to a personal matter that doesn't need to be discussed openly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me just to say one thing to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that I worked normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If he intends to talk about his health, maybe we should go back to the closed session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, we're back in open session. I want to ask you about something that you were asked on Monday. Page 24725 you were asked by Mr. Krgovic about any changes in the reporting rules or how things were done in 1992 after Mr. Drljaca came into the job as chief in Prijedor. And you said the reporting rules were the same in 1990 and in 1992, but they were not adhered to in 1992, thus, for instance, at times it was obligatory for us to hold morning briefings, where we superiors would be duty-bound to report our activities and then it would so happen they would tell us the meeting would not be held. Now, my question is: What reporting rules were you referring to and where are those found? Are there some reporting rules in the Law on Internal Affairs or are these something more informal and local?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules on the communications where I was an official, I mean there are rules, they are known, and they were held at the communications centre in their place. It was like a booklet or some kind of manual. As for the rules of work that I referred to a number of times and yesterday I used the term "police illiteracy" -- well, I really couldn't say that I read the whole thing but when I did come to the service in the 1980s as an engineer, I saw how the others were working and I did the same. Always those who came would learn from those who were already working. For example, if I went to another station on another kind of job I could see the people there working in the same way so that meant that really was the way the job should be done. Each police station had its own collegium, also the centre also had that. There would be a different make-up, though. As for where this was written, I really couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Between the time you started in 1980 and the time that Drljaca became the chief in 1992, how many different chiefs did you work for at SJB Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1982 until ... Simo came on the 30th in 1982 -- no, no, 1992, I'm sorry. Simo came on the 30th of April, 1992. Up until which date are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was between the time you began working in the police in 1980 until Drljaca came in 1992, how many different chiefs did you work for during those 12 years?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojan Panic from August until the new year, he retired; Rajko Zigic after him, one mandate for four years, and then another incomplete term of office for three years, that was the second one, he died; then Sead Besic came for a brief period, just briefly because they said that he had to go to Banja Luka to be the chief of the centre there. I don't know how short his term of office was, perhaps a couple of months. Then Slobodan Stojanovic came. And then the multi-party elections were held and then instead of Slobodan this Hasan Talundzic came. That was that. I don't think I've forgotten anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that when you worked under those prior chiefs at least up until Hasan came, did you have regular morning meetings or regular collegiums?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from day one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How about under Hasan, did he also have regular collegiums?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were not regular. They were not regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then under Drljaca, it sounds like you didn't have very many at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And "yes" meaning there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But one difference in addition to Drljaca being the new chief was that after April 30th there was a lot of combat and fighting going on in Prijedor after April 30th, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. Can you clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One thing that changed after April 30th, besides getting a new chief in Simo Drljaca, was that there was a lot of combat going on in Prijedor in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was fighting, but everything changed. A man came into the police force who had never been there unless he had been brought in by the policemen, and so on and so forth. There were many other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned after Mr. Drljaca became chief there were certain personnel changes within the SJB in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which you said is not unusual, that that often happens when there's a change in the chief; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really in the Socialist system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, at page 24726 when talking about this you said -- you mentioned a couple of specific changes and then you said: [As read] "There were similar examples like this one. It is the prerogative of a chief to move people around. The first thing that they always do is they always change their secretary." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, yes. That I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But let me ask you about that. The secretary for Hasan was Mira Topic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did think about it. I know that for a period of time she was there, but I am 1.000 per cent sure that she was there, Mira Topic, during that meeting on the 9th of April when Mr. Zupljanin came. Now I can't remember, there was either Sead or Hasan, one of those, who appointed a Muslim secretary who had earlier worked for the commander of the traffic police. She was there, but for a short time. And I can't remember whether it was Sead or Hasan who appointed her. What I do know is that Mira was there in those last days and stayed on when Simo was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll talk about her some more when we look at some of the communications logs because I think you indicated recognising her handwriting on some of the documents and some of the entries in the log-books from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 24726 and going on to 727 on Monday you were asked about some of the outlying police units being a part of the communications system, specifically about Ljubija, Kozarac, and Omarska. And you said they had an ultra short-wave radio set, a stationary one, and a telephone line as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you mentioned that none of those had a teleprinter, so you couldn't send them coded written information; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's right, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So how was written information sent from Prijedor to Ljubija, Kozarac, and Omarska? Just by courier?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A policeman would carry a great deal of things, not just dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: None of these were very far away from Prijedor, right, none of those three places?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozarac 12, Ljubija likewise, and Omarska perhaps 25 kilometres, not far away. By car, not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how often did couriers go? Did they go every day? Twice a week? Or just as often as necessary? How was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, officially I don't know, but let me also say that there was always somebody from that police station over here in town because they needed consultation, to see the commander, so there was constant communication. We were in contact or so -- in physical contact because we were close.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you mentioned that according to the organisational chart in the MUP in 1991/early 1992 that Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, and Bosanska Dubica were under Prijedor in terms of the communications. Am I saying that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat it briefly and then you'll see if your understanding is correct. Officially the organisation changed at times. At times Banja Luka was a centre for all of us, Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Dubica would in those circumstances be on equal terms vis-a-vis Banja Luka. Under a different organisation, Prijedor would become the centre, in which case the three municipalities would gravitate toward Prijedor. However, the technology was always in the hands of Prijedor. It never changed even though the organisational structure did, Prijedor was always in a superior position in relation to the other municipalities when it came to communications technology if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to understand is I have the understanding that when Banja Luka was sending out dispatches to Prijedor and its other SJBs, that communications that were intended for Sanski Most, Novi, and Dubica came to Prijedor and then Prijedor forwarded them on to those three SJBs. It didn't go directly from Banja Luka to Sanski Most; it went through Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Banja Luka is sending a dispatch to Sanski Most only, then it would go directly to Sanski Most. Technically speaking, it would go through Prijedor, but it would not go through any person's hands. It would merely go through the equipment. However, if Banja Luka was sending a dispatch to all the municipalities, then it was a circular and it would be sent from Banja Luka to Prijedor only and the operator in Prijedor would be forwarding a circular to all equally if everything worked as it should, which often was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that now. That's better. And if Sanski Most or Dubica or Novi wanted to communicate with Banja Luka, they had direct links to Banja Luka and they didn't have to go through Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what is important again is to stress that in organisational terms you're right; however, technically speaking, yes, if there was a malfunction in any place, like in Prijedor, again what I'm saying is it wouldn't go through any physical person. It would go through the technology itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you a document that maybe will help me understand a little better. It's Exhibit P1471. It's tab 3 of the Prosecution binder. This will come up on your screen in a minute. Let me know if you can read it there. It's a diagram I think of the telephone network in Bosnia before the war, before April of 1992. Can you see that all right or do we need to enlarge it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if text can be enlarged. I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think we need the bottom half right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see, we have the republican SUP in the middle and in the upper left quadrant you'll see CSB Banja Luka and Prijedor. Can you see that? I can hand you my copy if that's easier.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to read. Yes, please, if I could be given a copy and if I can read from that copy. Yes, excellent. I can see everything now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, have you seen that before, that diagram?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very old chart. It depicts what used to be the communications plan much, much earlier. It does not mean much without the supporting text. But you can ask me about it and I can see what it is that you've marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: The key has been translated for me. Banja Luka has a small circle within a bigger circle and that is explained to be a nodal switchboard. Do you understand that term and can you explain it to me?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there's the key at the bottom. Let me first note that the key and the designations are not universal. They were chosen by the author, but then we have the key so we can have a look at it and how it is logically. So I do understand it. The main switchboard and the nodal switchboard or the hub switchboard. The main switchboard was the SUP and Banja Luka was a node or a hub. If we wanted to explain it in somewhat broader terms, the main switchboard can get connected to anyone, whereas the hub or the node is just the node. What it connects. For instance, the CSB Banja Luka, how can they place a call to Vitez, CSB Zenica and then Vitez. They can do so via Sarajevo. That's why I say the main one can do whatever it wants, can get connected to anyone and the node needs to go through the main switchboard, if this is enough for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so. And on this diagram Prijedor is listed as a nodal switchboard as well and I take it that's because it has the ability to communicate directly with Sanski Most, Dubica, and Novi. That's why it's a hub?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not the main but the nodal switchboard. It is only Sarajevo that is the main one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was just saying corresponds to what we have here. I said that Prijedor could transmit circulars to these three municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you needed to get -- if you needed to get a written communication -- a coded written communication from Banja Luka to Sanski Most, could Banja Luka send that directly without any human being in Prijedor having to do anything with it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There existed in parallel to this transmission system that we see here a different system of encryption or cryptographic data protection. That particular chart or system could not be as extensive as this one. Why? Because every two participants have to have a document in order to be able to interact. Now, imagine how many participants there are and each interacting with the other. Well, there would be a roomful of these and you have that yellow tape with -- that is perforated. I don't know if you've seen that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, I have, about 40 years ago when I was in my army doing something I did see some of those things. But if I understand correctly, if Sanski Most and Banja Luka have the encryption device or the tape on each end, they also need a connection through which to send that message; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was such a link between Banja Luka and Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a link. There is the equipment, but there is no tape or ribbon under that organisational chart because what we have in Prijedor -- I'll say this very briefly to make it clear to you. You have two tapes or ribbons that form a pair. Let's say they are between you and me. And that there's two more between me and Sanski Most and that there's four ribbons or tapes, it's one I would have and then each would belong to one of the three municipalities. That's it. Nothing can happen unless you have a tape. You can have all the devices you want and all the equipment you want unless you have that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I and Sanski Most have the tape and you and Banja Luka have the corresponding tape, you can send me a message directly without any human being in Prijedor having to do anything with it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll talk some more about that later, but let me now go on sort of chronologically based on the questions that were asked of you Monday. You were talking at page 24729 about when Hasan Talundzic came to work as chief and one of the problems that you had with him was that he had no prior police experience; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you said also that he didn't consult with you on a regular basis. You said after he came you could only talk to your colleagues below you. You didn't have anyone upwards to consult with because he didn't do that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, he didn't have any knowledge about it. It wouldn't have made any sense to consult him because he had no knowledge of the things that we are discussing right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And he had -- and you said he also was doing most of his consulting with the local political authorities as far as you could see and not with policemen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you -- that sounds like you could say the same thing about Simo Drljaca when he came, no prior police experience, not consulting with you, and consulting with the local political authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say so yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The only difference is Talundzic is a Muslim and Drljaca was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And those who they went to to be told what to do were Muslims in one case and Serbs in the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. I think this would be a good time to take our first break for the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to spend a little time going through some of the log-books, communication log-books, from Prijedor. If I could with the usher's assistance hand you a binder with four or five of the log-books I want to talk about. I think you were shown some of these when you were interviewed by Mr. Yarmah and --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Banja Luka, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you open the binder you will see the first one has a tab number 129. That's the first one I want you to look at and I'll give you a specific page in a moment. This is Exhibit Number P2080, Your Honours. And, Witness, before you go could you look at the cover page of that document -- yeah, that -- the very first page -- yeah. Can you tell us what that word is on the cover of that notebook, the black page?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would just like to mention the basic things. In cryptographic work there is no term that would be used as a register or a notebook. There are books like that in other departments with the cleaning department or something, but I don't know anything about that. I never worked with books like that, log-books. This is a log-book of a sort. I opened it. I could see right away that it was from 1985. I recognised the signature of my former superior, Rajko Zigic. It says here authorised staff so this is what I said in relation to 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Staying on that page if we could. If we could go to page 3 of the B/C/S in e-court. And, Witness, it's the page you're looking at right now. We don't have an English translation of that. Could you read to us what it says on that page that you've got open in the book there. Yes. It has the big word in Serbian "delovodnik."

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Log-book, "delovodnik," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what else is written on that page on the top in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states Municipal Secretariat for Internal Affairs, Prijedor. That was our official name at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned it had a reference to 1985. I think that's where the first entry begins is in --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I only want to talk about 1992, and I've put a yellow stickie note at the place where 1992 begins in your hard copy -- no, at the top. Yes, that first yellow stickie note, if you could go to that page and in e-court that's -- in B/C/S that's page number 166, which matches up with the English page we have in e-court on the screen. Now, Witness, on that left-hand page do you see at the top I think it says "1992"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Looking at this, can you tell me what this book is about, which types of communications are logged in here. Is it incoming or outgoing and which department is keeping this book? Are you able to tell?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be hard. It would be very irresponsible for me to interpret anything because this is a document that I had nothing to do with. Only on the basis of my experience I can see that this is the handwriting of Mira Topic, the secretary. This is what I see, nothing more than that. I can see that it's her signature. She did enter some official documents but I don't know pursuant to what rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you would go to -- it's item number or transmission number 15. Do you find that? In the left-hand column --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- number, do you find number 15? Yeah, okay. My English translation says the subject of that is a plan for short-wave radio connections for the month of April 1992 dated the 30th of March and under distribution code it has your name; is that right? Can you tell us about that? Were there monthly plans for radio communications that were distributed to communication chiefs in the MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in a little bit. This is the KT plan so this is the short wave. I'm keeping my hand here, this is the KT radio connection and that connection actually is not used at all. This is just there as the last reserve in case all the other systems should break down, all the post offices, all the wires, then it just goes from device to device via antenna and you can, for example, set up a KT connection from Prijedor to Japan. And that is why the signals people, even though they didn't use that connection practically, they did hold trainings in order to keep up their skills to use the keyboard. So that is what the trainings were for. If you lose practice or if you are out of practice, you cannot use the keyboard. So, for example, the training centre would refer to something which sounds quite important. It's called the communication plan, but actually what it indicates is just at what time we should communicate and using which signals. For example, TFS, your name would be QI or whatever, I don't know. That's the plan actually. Has nothing to do with actual transfer of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm trying to find out in regard to this under the column that says "sender" it says CSB was the sender of this document and then it looks like you were the one who received it. Is that a fair reading of that entry?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the secretary received it she knew it was for communication, and then as the chief, as the head, I would receive that and then I would issue it to the workers who were working on that. So every day at a certain time we would establish communication at that particular frequency and that was just for the sake of keeping up the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll see in a minute, but it seems like many of the documents referred to in this particular log-book are longer documents. For example, this -- the one that you were just looking at, there's another one that's rules on internal organisation, a plan for confiscating weapons, a telephone or ultra short-wave directory. So these appear to be longer documents which I think you explained to me wouldn't be sent by Teletype. Those were the kind of things that would be sent by a courier because they were too long. Do you understand what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a lot mixed up in there. You mentioned weapons. I don't know which weapons. That has nothing to do with me. But as for the telephone connections and communications, yes, that has something to do with me. I would like you to be just a little bit more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm trying. Maybe I didn't form my question well. You'll see, we'll look at --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- we'll see on some other documents, but the nature of most of the documents that are listed in this log-book, they're not short one-paragraph, one-page document, like are sent as dispatches via Teletype. They're the longer documents which I think you explained in your earlier testimony were the kind of things that would not be sent by Teletype because they're too long and they're not secret, they're not urgent so they go by courier. It might be a 30-page document or a 50-page rule book. Do you understand so far?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is very broad so I really need to tell the story in order to answer the whole question. I don't know if you mean whether it was adopted, why -- I don't know what exactly the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Let's look at a couple and it may be that --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go to number --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one general remark. The papers that you've seen plenty of them of that particular kind, as the state of Yugoslavia we had the doctrine of All People's Defence, so the concept was that if anybody ever attacked us every village would have everything they needed and we would defeat anybody. So I myself really wasn't that familiar with all the documents, I didn't understand all of them, and I didn't use them all. However, there were professional National Defence services who were writing that. So they were showing the results of their work through all those papers so there were so many of those papers but when there was a need to use them none of them were used. Perhaps that's the sort of papers or documents that you looked at. If you can show them to me then I will talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me show you a couple of documents and I'll ask you some further questions. Could you look at number 19. I think it's the next page on for you. Item number 19, it's -- the subject described is plan for confiscation of illegally acquired or owned weapons and mines and explosives from groups and individuals in the Prijedor area. The date is 27 May. The sender is SJB Prijedor. It says three copies delivered to the CSB. And then in the far right column it says CSB Banja Luka to the CSB chief sent via colleagues from CSB, delivered by M. Djenadija. Do you know who M. Djenadija was, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you skipped two words and those two words are very important. Sent to the chief through colleagues from the CSB. So evidently this was not conveyed by any kind of communication. Okay, Djenadija, Marko, at the time was some kind of commander. I don't know -- I don't want to mix them up. Maybe he was at the police station number 2, the one in Urije. I don't know. They changed so really it's been a while. I can't tell anymore but he was some sort of komandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he had a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look on the screen for the moment at exhibit P1036. This is at tab 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, we're going to show you a document I think may relate to the log-book. You see, this appears to be a cover letter from Mr. Drljaca. It's addressed to the chief at Banja Luka, and my English translation says: "Please find herewith enclosed for further comment and approval the plan for confiscation of weapons ..." et cetera. And you see at the top the number of this communication is 11-12-19 dated the 26th of May, 1992. Can you explain for us again ABOUT the numbering system of communications within the RS MUP in 1992? What does the 11 stand for in that number?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know generally but I don't want to make any mistakes. But I can tell you the principle. Between the lines, the first part of the number talks about the organisational unit. 11, I think was at the time referring to Prijedor, that stood for Prijedor. 12 is a subunit, it could be the chief that's separate, then the police station, the criminal investigations police, communications, and so on and so forth. And the next one, the last one should be the log-book, log number. I mean, to me that's a foreign term, but I think that should be the number there. Did we say 19? Yes, that's it. Let's say by hierarchy, company Prijedor, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll look at some more. I know it's been a long time since you dealt with these, but I would suggest to you that 11 seems to refer to CSB Banja Luka. And 11-12 refers to Prijedor SJB.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're most probably right because as you were speaking I remembered. When we were part of the Banja Luka centre - and that's that period - then the centre was the first number, so 11 then would be Banja Luka and then Prijedor would be 12. But, however, here this number is kind of small. There were more numbers. The number should have the chief, criminal investigation police, perhaps communications. My number was 04 and so on and so forth. And then the last number would be the log-book number. So this number is very short. So I cannot really tell what goes with what in terms of the police departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. We'll look at numbers that are longer. And is it correct, most of the time I'm used to seeing on the end of a number on a document like this a slash and the year, two-digit year, 92, 93, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the year, yes. And these longer ones I forgot about them even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go back to the log-book, I want to show you another one, Exhibit P2080 and for you it's item number 20, the very next item in the book. You were looking at 19, if you could look at 20 -- no, it's still on the same page, I think, where you were. You were looking at number 19. Look at the very next one, number 20. It's -- my translation says the subject is order regarding treatment of arrested persons. Sender is SJB Prijedor. It's delivered to the Crisis Staff, some co-ordinators, a couple words are not translated because they're illegible according to our interpreters. But the name Jasic, Majstorovic, Banja Luka CSB, chief of security, administrator of the iron ore mines and archives. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just keep that number 20 in mind and I want to show you another document and that's P1560, that's tab 58 on the Prosecution's list. I can give you a hard copy of this one with some help from the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a general objection to the line of questioning by Mr. Hannis, because this witness is being shown a document that is not a communications document and he's being asked to look at the document and to read what it says. But it's already been admitted so what would be the purpose of this line of questioning of this witness? Just to read what it states in the document and to confirm that that's what is written. It's not a communications document so I don't know how that can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it goes to a host of issues. This witness worked in the SJB in Prijedor and although he was the head of communications I believe it's fair to assume that he had some fair knowledge about the general workings of the police station. He knows various individuals, he recognises handwriting, and I think he can shed some light on how books were kept, what kinds of information were received by whom, how they were distributed, et cetera. And he can also comment on the content of a number of these documents, at least as to whether he knew about them or not. And the level of his knowledge is going to be very important in assessing the credibility of all his evidence at the end of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so, Mr. Hannis. One thing that struck me, though, is that apart from the basis of Mr. Krgovic's observation that the documents which have been admitted speak for themselves, the witness's answer to some of your earlier questions, having indicated his unfamiliarity with the contents, as it were, seeing these exhibits for the first time, I wonder how much usefulness is going to be derived from the line of questions that you propose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps I could ask the witness to take his headphones off while I respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, could you take your headphones off for a minute while I speak to the Judge about something. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, communications apparently still appears to be a hotly contested issue in this case, at least from the Defence perspective. We think there is lots of evidence about communications and although there was evidence about electric part of communications not working, we say there are lots of other ways to do communications, regular mail, courier, et cetera. This witness was not in a position to know about all those, but he can corroborate that these documents are from Prijedor, that he recognises signature of the secretary of the chief on some of these documents. So they're authentic and they reflect that communications were going on beyond and above and outside what's in the communication log-books per se. This is not a communication log-book that was kept in his centre; rather, it appears it was one kept by the chief's secretary. But it reflects communications that won't show up that he hasn't seen. So we need to supplement his evidence about the level and quantity of communications with other evidence, otherwise we're left with him saying: Oh, communications didn't work and, you know, it was terrible and we weren't able to communicate with anybody to the extent that he said something like that. And I think we're entitled and it's necessary for me to try and establish that that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can put your headphones back on. This relates to what I was asking before about lengthy documents. This is more than just one or two pages, this document, so I understand from your earlier evidence this is not something that would have been transmitted electronically through your communications system simply because of the length of the document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the gentleman from the OTP asked me about this. I don't remember literally what I said, but I repeat it because I want to say it. The rule of transfer of written information is that half a page up to one page of text can be transferred by teleprinter. Everything else is conveyed by courier. That's the rule. However, often because of the urgency, even two or three pages if necessary are sent, if they have to be sent, but this did not constitute a rule. And usually the signals operator would ask for my opinion. If it has to be sent then it would be typed. It's not a problem, you could send two or three pages, but never 10 pages or 20 pages. If that's what you meant. I said that before and I'm repeating that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any documents from Chief Drljaca addressed to the Crisis Staff? Did any of those documents ever get sent via the communications centre that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not through the communications centre. That's because the Crisis Staff is nearby, and as for me monitoring or keeping track of these things on any other basis, no, that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go now to the next tab in your binder, tab number 130. Thank you. Tab number 130 and if you could tell me -- this is Exhibit P2088. Can you read for us what's written on the cover of that book or printed on the cover of that book in Serbian because we don't have an English translation of that cover page?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book of outgoing coded telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you look at the next page in B/C/S in e-court and the inside cover, could you look at the next page in your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what's there, the stamp and the printed words?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book contains 100 sheets of paper with the numeration between 1 and 100 and bound and I'm -- I signed it as head of the communications and KZ, that's encryption section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So was this a book that was kept in your communications centre in Prijedor SJB in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This book is obviously an official document containing records of coded documents that the centre transmitted. As I said yesterday, it normally had its official designation, the form, and it does say, in fact, K20, but what I see here that it's not really the book of records of our centre but rather of the chief's secretary. Let me explain this further, the secretary, the administrative secretary, was duty-bound to keep a separate record of her own of all these coded dispatches. Since she didn't have a notebook of her own to do this, I gave her the book that we normally used. Since the book is one of coded dispatches encrypted, it has to be bound in this way. You can't really tell it here because you can't see it, but it's the way of binding a book in such a way that the sheets of paper cannot be taken out, cannot be interchanged. This is part of the cryptographic data protection system. And you can also see that it's her handwriting here so she made the entries. And in column number 7 you can see the signatures of the various individuals who actually worked under me, they were various encryption operators. I know their names. So she would note down the date and time of a dispatch, the person who received it, and so you have all the information there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This particular book then, where was it kept? Was it kept in the secretary's office or in the communications centre or the chief's office? Physically, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the beginning of your question was cut off. I didn't hear it. Can you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure. This particular book, where was it physically kept in 1992? Was it in the communications centre --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was kept by the secretary, the personal assistant. I never checked this book. I gave her an empty notebook and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that would be Mira Topic that we've talked about before?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the date here is back in 1986 and I think it was Nada Markovska who occupied the post and not Mira Topic. Well, at any rate, in these various times a lot of them changed. I don't know how many. I don't think this is Mira's signature. It may have been Nada, who if I remember correctly, was there first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake. Can you go to the yellow stickie note, go to that one and I think that will take you to the entries for 1992 in this particular log-book begin.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's page number, I believe, 19 in e-court. It's ERN P0042544 do you recognise the writing in 1992, is that Mira Topic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most of them, yes, but there are entries where it is not her from what I can tell. Under 19 that doesn't seem to be her, but item 6, for instance, 7 as well, or rather, from 1 to 10, yes, that's Mira Topic. I am certain that it is her. Maybe somebody will say that it isn't, but I'm sure that that's not her under 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Could you go to the very next page -- or actually, can you go two pages further on and two pages further on in e-court. I want you to look at item numbers 49, 50, and 51 -- I'm sorry, I may have sent you too far. Can you go back and find the items 49, 50, and 51. Looks like telegram numbers 2023, -25, and -31. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The signature for item number 49, that appears to be Goran. Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the communications officers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you repeat his family name for us.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: K-o-v-r-l-j-a, Kovrlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now is --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm sorry, there is an "I" missing, K-o-v-r-l-i-j-a, so his name is Kovrlija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It appears that the numbers assigned to these dispatches are in ascending order, numerical order. Where does the assignment of numbers come from? How do you know what number to put on the next outgoing telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the last number -- let me think it over rather than make a mistake. I'm trying to remember these things. It was a long time ago. Normally the number in its entirety, which is found within the heading of any typical dispatch, the former part would be written by the author and the last four digits would have been added by the communications officer dealing with the dispatch. And those would normally be added by hand. Since this is Mira's book and the numbers are not in sequence and they are not even Mira's as far as I can tell by looking at the handwriting - and this is me making an inference - I believe that Mira left this particular box empty whenever she prepared a dispatch and wanted to take it over to the communications and encryption section, she would fill in all these save for that number, time, and signature. And then the communications officer would use the first next number available in his book and Mira would take it over and write it in here and she would write the date when she handed the dispatch over and ask the operator on duty to place his signature there. That's how things should have worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But the book where the running list of numbers is kept is in the communications centre? Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. In the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And because it appears there are only 100 coded telegrams sent in 1992 with the first one having a number of 141 and the last one having a number of 2.580, that means there's something like 2.480 other numbers in that range from 1 to 2.580 that weren't coded telegrams. What documents did those other numbers go to, if you follow my question? Open telegrams? Other kinds of communications that aren't telegrams --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is clear and now let me tell you. As I said, the book was of the format which belonged to cryptographic data protection. All the other rules related to encryption stemmed from those prescribed by the army. We were called upon to adhere to those. We were just one group of users of those. Having said that, as I said, the books were not destroyed before the expiry of one year or -- well, one year at the most. They could have been destroyed after six months as well. So what happened next? Since we had a very low fluctuation of dispatches because we were a small station, if I only filled in two of the sheets, two of the pages, and the rest of the book was empty, the practice was that we would if we had a lot of these books in stock, we would have this one destroyed to adhere to the rules. However, it also happened that we would continue using that book and that was the case with this because you see that the book stretches from page 88 to, or rather, from year 1988 to 1996. So it was -- it had a long life and this was actually contrary to the rules. Had we had an inspection come in, they might have had understanding for this and perhaps not. I have not had experience with the inspection looking into this sort of rules. So I can't tell you what the case was in this -- with this specific book. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think we had a miscommunication. I think you were explaining why we have more years than just 1992 in the book, but my question is: Focusing on the year 1992, just the year 1992, in there we see there were 100 telegrams, coded telegrams, sent in the entire year 1992 from Prijedor SJB with the first number --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the chief, but if it was the commander who was sending a dispatch and believed that it had to be coded, it would be designated as coded but it would not be entered into this book. Or, for instance, if I sent out a coded telegram from the communications centre, it would not have been entered into this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll look at your year-end report on communications later and come back to this issue. But do you understand the point I'm making about the -- the last number that went out on a telegram, for example, before the /92 at the end of the number? It appears that in 1992 the first document that went out would have been 11-12-something/01. But the first telegram that went out, the first coded telegram that went out in 1992 appears to have been on the 6th of January and it was given the number 141, do you see that, very first entry for 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6th January, 1992, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it was number 141; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: What were numbers 1 through 140 before the 6th of January? What kind of documents would those numbers have been assigned to, if you know? Something other than a coded telegram obviously?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now the question is clear to me. Since I've forgotten all the details, let me -- I would have said at first that these were only coded dispatches. But if we have 141 -- if I look at that number I say that there's not a chance that they could all have been coded. There must have been open ones among them. Did I understand this now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe. Let me ask you another question. Does that mean then that in total - because you'll see the last number in that log-book is I think 2.580 - does that mean to you that in 1992 the total number of coded telegrams and open telegrams sent from Prijedor SJB must have been at least 2.580?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Things change. It's very difficult. There are four numbers in the books, those received, those transmitted, those open, and those protected. And it changed. And at times during the war the total number would have been over 100.000. However, at the time when this arrived, there would have been a thousand at the most. So thinking about these approximations, I know that we had over 100.000 dispatches, but most of them were open. Those were the peaks, let's say. But I couldn't give you the figures, not even approximate ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you stay with me for a little bit. Look at the last page, telegram number 100 for -- can you go to number 100 for 1992. If you'll -- you'll have to keep turning your page, I think. It should be the last page. There you go, on the right-hand side, the right-hand page. Witness, the other -- see number 100?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's been assigned the number 2580, 2.580, on the 30th of December, 1992. To me that suggests that in 1992 there were 2.579 other documents before this. We see by this book that 100 documents in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that 100 of those documents are coded telegrams, the ones in that book. But you also have open telegrams. So am I right in assuming that there were 2.000 -- at least 2.480 open telegrams sent in 1992, to make up for all those numbers that aren't in this book? Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question clearly and I clearly understand what it is that you want. And I'm trying to wrack my brains to recall all these things. And I'm trying to recall the way these books were kept, such as this book of outgoing dispatches.
