It is true to a large degree that all the dispatches received by a communications operator received in terms of the fact that he had to transmit them further, they would get the next available number. And then there would be a designation indicating whether they were open or protected. So it logically arises from this book that by this date the total of 2.580 dispatches were sent, of which 100 were sent only from the chief, but that does not mean that they were all coded telegrams. Jankovic could have sent coded telegrams to Banja Luka and they would not have been noted here. So I believe we have resolved this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think so. Thank you. Now if you could go to the tab 132, not the very next one but the second one after in your book, yeah, behind 132.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's Exhibit P2090.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you look at the first page. That doesn't tell you much. I think it just says CSB Banja Luka on it. If you could turn inside --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And inside do you recognise any of the handwriting or the numbering on those pages? It appears to be some sort of courier or mail delivery log-book. You've never seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Not even with your colleague who brought over these things. I don't know anything about it. However, this title, working lists, well, this is something that we had in our encryption work. So I suppose that this is something that they used for handling their papers. It is similar to what we had in our department, but this is the first time I see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell me about couriers. Did you have couriers in the police in Prijedor SJB in 1992; and if so, were they part of your department or were they just regular policemen who did that duty or were they part of the duty operations service? Who were the people who actually delivered hard copies to mail back and forth between Banja Luka and Prijedor, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period before when everything was normal -- may I begin my answer? Very well. Earlier on, as I say, when everything was normal, definitely before the multi-party elections, there was a plan for the courier service and I think it was normally on Tuesdays and Thursdays that a policeman from the duty service would go to Banja Luka and come back, but they had nothing to do with me in organisational terms. If I needed to have anything sent, I would get in touch downstairs with the secretary of the chief and ask when the courier was due and I would send the envelope with him and he would deliver it to whoever I needed. It was the police or the commander, I don't know who it was, who decided when these things would be sent out. Now there arose a huge problem of the shortage of petrol. So everybody was economising on this. The chief was not able to provide the sufficient amount of petrol. So everything was done to make sure that the courier was not sent to Banja Luka for any little errand. If I needed to have anything sent, I would then use their services, but it was rarely that I would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I understand you started that answer talking about before the war, was the system with couriers still generally the same after April 30th, 1992? I take it they went as often as was necessary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just told you, the system remained the same. But even where everything remains the same, if there is no petrol, then nothing is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm sorry, I didn't understand that. Thank you. Okay, I think I've lost my audience a little bit so let's not talk about log-books for a while and switch to something else.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was no petrol and economising with petrol and vehicles and personnel. There was a shortage of personnel as well so we had a number of problems, not just one. Under such circumstances, the chief and the commander had to organise things and it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you now about something else you talked about on Monday. You were at page 24730 talking about the tensions in town in April/May of 1992, both before -- well, let's talk about before the Serb take-over and the first month or so immediately after. You mentioned that one could feel that in the town and that there were people who didn't react the same way. You had a colleague and you maintained good relations. What particular colleague were you talking about that you maintained a good relationship with after the Serbs took over, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were plenty that I maintained a good relationship with. I don't know. Well, anyway, if I was thinking of my colleague with whom I was on good terms with and then there was a certain cooling, I think that this was perhaps Ago Sadikovic, this was an inspector who worked with my wife on white collar crime. But there was also Suljo Dzonlagic who was my colleague from university, he was a neighbour within an engineer as well. He taught in school. Until the end I was on good terms with him because those who were friends for a longer period with Suljo, for example, our friendship was never jeopardised, but with Ago there was a kind of cooling in relations without any quarrel or conflict. It's different from person to person. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those that you just mentioned, do you know if any were detained and taken to Keraterm or Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Ago because he didn't sign for that thing in the morning when he came. I don't know afterwards, I didn't see him after that. He didn't even live close to me. As for Suljo, he didn't go to Keraterm or Omarska. He managed to join some kind of convoy or something and now he's in Sydney, I mean he was in Austria somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about Nusret Sivac, did you know him? He worked in the state security in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can ask me about him as much as you want. I was his boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him after the -- [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him after the Serbs took over in Prijedor? Wasn't he detained and kept at Keraterm or Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sivac was detained twice. I don't know if that's in his statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know where he was detained and how he was treated when he was there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like this, Sivac was a signals operator just like the others. There is that book by Mira Topic from earlier on. I think there are signatures by him there too until 1989 and then he retired. The book that we had before this one, there are signatures by Sivac there. I think you can check that that was until the end of 1989 and then he went -- he retired because he wanted to and also because he had the legal condition. Sivac was always a communications operator and I was his boss, officially. Unofficially, Sivac was carrying around a film camera and recorded or taped things part time and sent it to Sarajevo television. He made short news items from Prijedor. Usually in the TV crew there would be -- the journalist who would be the one in charge, but he turned that around. So he was the main person in the crew and he would always find a journalist. So the journalists would change but Sivac would always be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, let me stop you because my question was do you know where he was detained and how he was treated when he was there? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say that. I was about to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Sivac -- and Sivac was detained, he wasn't working those days that were bad when people were being detained, I didn't have any contact with him. But then later he said when we met that he was taken away - I don't know who took him away - he was taken to Omarska. Omarska was already set up by then. He wasn't detained before that. As far as I know he wasn't brought in to the SUP, to the police, either. Perhaps he was, but as far as I know he wasn't. He was taken to Omarska and there was an interview with him there and then in a day or two Sivac was released as not guilty. But then he was in Prijedor for a few days, I don't remember how many, and then he was detained again because allegedly in the investigation some new circumstances were established. And I think that he told me that he was there for 40 days. Perhaps he wasn't. I don't know. I can't remember that. In any event, Sivac was released after his second stay and then he came to me asking me for help. He said that he wanted to go somewhere, I don't know, Germany, somewhere in Europe with his own vehicle. He happened to have a Ford Escort. He had a wife and two children. The children were just like my children, 7 and 10 years old, something like that. And as I said, at the time there was no petrol so these people - how shall I put it? - not from the police but those people who were not respecting the laws, they would seize a car from somebody for as long as there was petrol in it and then they would just discard it and take a new one. So close to some creche next to the SUP I saw his car just there. I just noticed it by accident. And then he came to me and he said, "Boss" -- he was afraid to come, he was scared to come. I mean, he had no reason to be afraid, but I guess he did. If he was afraid, well then let him be afraid. He asked if I would be able to somehow get this car to him because he wanted to go. I said I would try. I didn't do it myself, I sent a technician, Mladen Raus to find out who was driving that car, it was somebody close to the SUP, some kind of reserve soldier or police officer. In any case, he found the keys to the car, took the car to Sivac, and Sivac used that car to go to Europe. This is it in brief. I don't know where he went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that was -- that was more than brief I think. You've indicated to us you are quite detailed and meticulous --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because I have limited time, I'll have to ask you from time to time to try and keep your answers short and if I need more I will ask more. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you just give me a sign with your hand and I will cut it short. It's not a problem. I'm trying to adjust it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, thank you. You said you weren't sure what Mr. Sivac was afraid of. Wasn't he afraid of the kind of thing that was happening to non-Serbs in Prijedor at the time, that he might be arrested and detained again without any criminal charges being filed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was afraid. But, sir, I was also lying down on a stone in front of these semi-savage Serbs. Somebody hit me a number of times over here. I was afraid as well. Perhaps Sivac was a little bit more or a little bit less afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I remember you telling us about the incident where you were shot at as well.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You talked --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just that. I was hit by a rifle when I was coming back from Omarska, not hit, I was beaten by brother Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Army? Police? What?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that even they don't know who they were. They had old JNA uniforms from Comrade Tito times. Somebody had trousers, somebody had a shirt, it was an odd combination, somebody didn't have any of the uniform items. They did have weapons, though, but this was the military I think, not the police. The police knew me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned I think before that you visited Omarska three times. Which one of your three visits did this happen on, the first, second, or the third?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first, the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see it's nearly time for our break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would return at 12.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, on Monday when you were talking about the situation in Prijedor after the take-over on 30 April, you talked about a number of the non-Serbs or mostly Muslims leaving. And you talked specifically at page 24735 about a communications worker under you, Mirsad Sahuric, did I pronounce his name correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: S-a-h, Sahuric, you pronounced it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I seldom hear that. You mentioned that he was probably one of the last ones to leave, but while he was there you said: [As read] "I tried to the best of my ability to make it as comfortable for him to stay in that environment. I tried as best I could to help him. There were other colleagues and I as well who helped him to get food-supplies because they were people who did not dare to walk about the town." What was it in Prijedor after the 30th of April, 1992, that made it so uncomfortable for the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say. I'm going to try to be brief. I mean, this is a complex question. One would need to write a serious study about it but it's impossible to explain it in ten sentences. But I will do my best. The gist, and I always say that not just here, everywhere, it's not that the Serbs are no good or the Muslims are good or the other way around. It's not a battery with a plus or a minus end. You cannot have a big one and a small one. They're always the same but they're opposites. After the 30th of April, the day this guy was killed, Japa [phoen], on that night, somebody killed him, a Muslim, but we never found out who it was. And the process began. Every day, every minute, there was a chance you could get killed no matter who you were. For example, I concluded for me it would be better not to wear a uniform because if I wore a uniform before the war, I didn't have the right to one during the war. I did. But if I wore a uniform there was a chance I could be hit by some residential building by some Muslim. They didn't leave, they were still there, they didn't reconcile them to the situation. Some people are staying, some are leaving, some people want to go and there was more and more shooting, there were more and more dead people of all ages from all ethnic groups. And that's why I say I never took a uniform. Perhaps it was better for some of my people from the police to stop me and search me without a uniform rather than to be in a uniform. So that situation wasn't any better or worse than any other situation. And in all of that, this is the main thing, there were shortages of power. When there's no electricity, you know what happens. Trade was dwindling down. There were shortages. There was no petrol, there was no bread. I happened to have my wife's parents living in a village nearby, some 15 kilometres away, I mean it's doable by bike. I couldn't use the car, there was no petrol. So I would go by bike. I would get some bread, some vegetables and that's how we lived. There were no salaries being paid. So in all of that some people had it good, they made it through, and some didn't. As time passed, however, and then on the 30th of May when that came around with that attack, then there was a selection that started to be made. Before then there was no selection. They were not bringing in citizens, they were just bringing in suspects for existing incidents, but there was no systematic thing. Then with the 30th, with the attack on Prijedor, it all began suddenly so that when I started to listen to the other side through the media, then I could see how the evil Serbs couldn't wait to start catching the poor Muslims. That is not correct. Earlier when you mentioned Nusret Sivac, he was not an innocent lamb that was brought to Omarska. He came back for the second time when he was telling me about this vehicle for me to try to get it back for him, he told me: "Well, boss, I spent" -- I don't know how many days he said he spent in Omarska for nothing. I said: "No, Nusret, that is not true. On the 30th of May you were in Obala." I am telling you Obala is a restaurant around which there was a large battle and one hero of theirs, one of their men was killed and then Kaduc [phoen], a Serb after whom a square now is named in Prijedor. So there were some battles and that's where Sivac happened to be. And I said, "How come you were there?" And he said, "Well, boss, I came to pick up the money from my private personal slot machine." So I don't know after all he was released twice he could have encountered some fool and something else could have happened and similar things happened to other people in other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understood when you asked to be able to go on a bit that it's not a simple question to answer and even though you did go on a bit, you didn't precisely answer the question I was asking which was what it was about that made it hard for the non-Serbs, the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask me, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I think I got part of your answer that did address that. I guess after the 30th of May when there had been the attack on Prijedor by Muslims then it sounds like you're saying there was a much more systematic rounding up of all kinds of Muslims, not just suspects. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the translation. Could you answer again. I don't think we got a translation.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of the question, what happened and what is the uncomfortable thing for those who are not Serbs before Serbs -- I mean, it's the same answer to the question of what happened to those who were not Muslims in areas where the Muslims were a majority, for example, in some other location. I mean, you could write a book about it. That is the essence, though it is complex. Okay. That's the first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I rephrase the question and maybe it will be easier -- maybe it's easier to answer this way. Is it fair to say in Prijedor municipality in areas where Muslims were a majority, it was difficult for non-Muslims because there was the danger of harassment, discrimination, even violence? And likewise in the Serb majority parts of Prijedor it was uncomfortable and dangerous for non-Serbs for the same reasons, because there were extremist Muslims and there were extremist Serbs. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, but if you permit me, I will add something. I will try to be as brief as possible. I always think that for anyone who wants to look at that situation without dwelling on this, then that look is incomplete. There is no town or place or area in Bosnia and Herzegovina and most probably in Yugoslavia, just like the area of Prijedor and Kozara, where the most recent past from World War II is so horrible. According to some data, I cannot really talk about that, but the numbers stayed with me. 19.472 children from that area were either killed or expelled. I'm talking about children now. To the -- compared to 20- to 30.000 adults. So this was during World War II. There is no house in that area, in the area where I was born all of this that we are talking about makes no sense because there were no casualties. In this area there is no Serbian home that does not have at least one horrible story to tell. And so this then arises in this semi-literate villager. It would be the same thing as if I, for example, was afraid of having AIDS or some sort of horrible disease because they were in a war before that and before that and so on. And just one more thing. I don't like to bring out examples all the time, but I think it's important briefly, and I'm not going to mention examples anymore, if you permit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment when I took the dispatch there and read it, I wasn't so crazy and unaware of the situation and many times when it was dangerous, but all I had in my head was one guiding thought. I mean, it wasn't a thought so much as an emotion and emotions never lead to happiness in such a situation and that is the following. A few days before the start of the war I went out for a walk with my son, who at the time was 5 or 6 years old and I met an old fighter from World War II, a Partizan, Mladjo Stanic who didn't know me, but I knew him because there's only one Mladjo, and there are many such as I, myself. I didn't ask him anything and he was speaking and he was already a bit off his rocker, mentally. So I didn't ask him anything but he was going and speaking, "These people in the municipality are fools" - and he meant the multi-party assembly - "I have been telling them why are you fighting? You will cause a war and they don't want to listen to me and because of these" - and he showed -- pointed to my child - "in 1941 so-and-so called me or let me know," he mentioned the names in Kozara, "they took away the children towards the Krecane, the local Ustashas caught them. I was running behind them with my fighters to catch up with them, but they had already killed the children. One male child they had impaled on a small pine and it was plucking at the blades of grass and I am still all shaken up about it." It's a horrible story and I cannot forget it to this very day and it's much worse for those whose forefathers, their grandfathers, were a part of that. Perhaps some of them can restrain themselves and some of them cannot. Because all of this -- this is a very uncommon region and everything that can be critically looked at from the side has to be looked at in the light of what applies to them is one thing and that does not apply to everybody else, it's just not the same situation. This is how I see things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand what you're saying there. But because of those -- those kinds of strong feelings, wasn't it -- not only was it in Prijedor hard for your former coworker Mr. Sahuric, it was also difficult for you, wasn't it, as a Serb to try and help a non-Serb because that was just as dangerous in a way. Those Serbs who had hard feelings about the Muslims and made life hard for them in Prijedor would make life hard for you if they found out you were helping a non-Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. However, a person always builds a defence mechanism of sorts. I believe in God and I believe that if I do good that I will fare well. And I also know that a good person cannot get in harm's way, I don't know why. But most of the time it turns out to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me now go and talk about April 9th. This is the meeting that you told us about that you had the notes from. Do you remember that? We looked at your handwritten notes --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, what I said or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had some questions based on what you said on Monday. I wasn't clear about a few things. At page 24.755 you mentioned that: [As read] "Somebody brought a prototype of the badge to show what it would look like." I think this was the three-coloured flag, the wavy flag that you mentioned. Do you remember who that was who brought that insignia and showed it at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say "someone." Perhaps you didn't hear it. It was Mr. Zupljanin who brought it along. That's the feeling I have. Yes, that was him. He said that that was the symbol that was proposed for this police force of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I wasn't clear on what it was. And then you said: [As read] "I think that the chief didn't even take the badge for himself. He gave it to Zijad Basic and said, 'Your wife is a Serb. Why don't you take the badge?'" Which chief were you talking about there, Talundzic or Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Zupljanin, I think it was him, yes. I do allow for the possibility that I am mistaken, but that's the way I remember things. After the meeting Zijad was showing us the badge and he was pleased. He wasn't angry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your note, I think one of the last notes you had a remark that you said referred to your own comments and you said you spoke about the concrete agreement or the specific agreement for us to be united. What specific, concrete agreement were you referring to when you said that? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you now, it was there at the meeting that we were supposed to come to an agreement, not that we were supposed to draw up an official agreement. Rather, that we were supposed to come to an agreement through our discussions, to be united, to have a single voice, to have the Prijedor station as part of the centre. Why would we be an island within a region? It was in that context that I mentioned it. I don't recall these words specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that in relation to what I think you had reported that Mr. Zupljanin said "you all," meaning you police in Prijedor needed to resolve it among yourselves about whether or not you were going to go with Banja Luka or go with Sarajevo. Was it in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a compound question or perhaps a bit complex. I'm afraid I didn't understand it. The story boiled down to the chief saying that we were supposed to arrange our relations within the centre. He didn't say you do it. He said, "We will set about doing it. We have the badges proposed here. All the other municipalities have agreed to it. We hope you will as well." That's the gist of it and then there was later on the decision that Prijedor and Kotor Varos would be exempted. It was within that context that the conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you explained a little bit about the notes that you took and you said that you acquired a habit over the time of making "... such cryptic notes that would be clear only to me and nobody else. For that reason it makes no sense to seek something and to read into this document. I'm the only one who can make use of that document." I understand that way of doing things. I've done that myself. But let me ask you: Have you ever had the experience of going back after a long period of time and looking at some of your cryptic notes and not being able yourself to remember what the cryptic parts meant? Does that ever happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in some other notes, not this set. Perhaps one in a hundred, very rarely, and it doesn't apply to these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That was my next question.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was younger it never happened, but now it does more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Welcome to the golden years. You said that -- then you were asked after this meeting if there were any changes that occurred before the end of April, and specifically about whether the Serb insignia or these new tri-coloured flag insignia were used. And you said: [As read] "No, they were not attached. As far as I know we received a dispatch from the centre saying that Prijedor and Kotor Varos" --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surely not before the take-over. Afterwards, yes, but I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit 2D18. This is tab 60 in the Prosecution binder. I can hand you a hard copy. Sorry, the record said tab 6-0 but I meant 16, 1-6. This is a dispatch from CSB Chief Zupljanin. Is this the one you were referring to? It's dated the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I remember is that there was a dispatch and that the message was what is written here. I suppose it dates back to the discussions I had with a representative of the Prosecution. I don't remember anything else. But it must be the dispatch. I don't think there's any other. This does not refer to Prijedor and comes from this time-period. That I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you'll see in the body of the text, I think it's the fourth paragraph referring to the insignia, it said that: "The obligations do not apply to the Prijedor and Kotor Varos SJB. They can continue to wear the current insignia until the political situation in these municipalities is solved." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the way the political situation in Prijedor was resolved was two weeks later the Serbs took over; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a political question. Please don't put political questions to me. I have no knowledge of that. It would be very irresponsible of me to say either way. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did the take-over of power bring? Was it good or bad things? Time will show. I don't know. Things were different; that much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for anything else, I think people wiser than me should be the ones to judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But really, Mr. Jankovic, between the 16th and the 30th of April, there wasn't like any free election in Prijedor about whether or not our police should wear this new insignia; right? The thing that happened was that there was a take-over by the Serbs on the 30th. That's how the situation was resolved and the police started wearing the tri-coloured insignia; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. Is this a question you're putting to me? To me it is a political statement you're putting to me rather than a question. Please ask me a question and I'll try and answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll ask you another question that's more in your field. At the top we see a number of names written and at the very top the letter R. Can you tell me what that refers to? Does that have to do with distribution of this message?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. It was written by the secretary. The letter R is short for "raspis," which stands for distribution. You would copy this and distribute among a number of recipients. And then I can read out the names for you, if this means anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions first. The Serbian word you use, "raspis," I think has been translated into English before as "circular". I don't know if I can inquire of the interpreters if that's right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by function it is similar, very similar. Let's say we have this one document and I have to send it to five recipients, so I make five copies and distribute the document to them. So in a way, yes, you could say that it was a circular.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Not necessarily the immediate translation of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And thank you, Witness. In this case, "R" refers to what? To whom else was this message sent? Did this thing go to Sanski Most and Novi and ... ?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. When such a handwritten note is made by the secretary, it is only for our purposes. I think it was the secretary, Mira, who made this note and I don't know who wrote the word "raspis." It may have been Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I thought maybe it was the secretary, Mira, but I see M. Topic is listed as one of the persons on here --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is her handwriting, whereas this other is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where you're pointing to is the top middle where it has the number 11-12/363 and the date of 16 --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Mira's handwriting, yes, yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. On the right --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whereas this other definitely is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And on the right that Jankovic, that first one, is that Dusan?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you're the one that's M. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos, M.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Kadiric was the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Fikret, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... who was Mihic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihic was the head of the crime police, those who were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the other two names under you, who were they? Temcuk, Sormaz?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This tells us something else. The first row above the line lists the individuals who are more important, whereas those below the line are not as important. Jankovic, that's me, Rada is the person from the accountancy service, the one who was in charge of the payroll, works for the police but is not an authorised official. That was Rada Temcuk, finances Ranka Sormaz, she was charged with identity cards, passports, et cetera. So she was unimportant, just as I was. And OM, 3 copies, that's for the three branches or substations, namely Ljubija, Kozarac, and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you a related document to that, it's P651 at tab 17 of the Prosecution's binder and with the usher's help, I'll hand you a hard copy and trade you for the one you've got right now. This one is also dated the 16th of April and it appears to come from Chief Hasan Talundzic and it appears that he's simply forwarding that one that we were just looking at. So is this one that was forwarded on from Prijedor to Sanski Most, Novi, and Dubica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a follow-up on the story from the previous document, where I said distribution or circular, where a number of copies had to be made -- well, this is one of those copies. It's just that on the others that were sent you wouldn't have Temcuk as the addressee but others. As I said, we were the public security station and Hasan Talundzic was in charge of our station only. The Sanski Most station was an independent one. Perhaps they received this dispatch from the centre. I am not in a position to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So who did this go to from the chief? Is this just an internal memo in Prijedor SJB or who does it get circulated to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. Within the CSB and the list of addressees was contained in the previous document, you were able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So here where it says "circular letter" it refers simply to those people we saw named on the last document and nobody else in Prijedor SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If I can add something, we had the line in the previous document where it said "3x OM," there had never been three police substations. Ljubija was always a station and apparently the author of the document was unaware of this. It was most probably Hasan, since he had been there for a very short time and he was a superior of an organisation he was not familiar with. Those who were more knowledgeable and experienced would not have written something like that. Of course physically it was Mira writing it up, but he chose the numbers -- I mean the names that were amongst the addressees in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Judge Harhoff, when you were talking about the April 9th meeting, at page 24768, asked you about Mr. Zupljanin exempting Prijedor and Kotor Varos from having to wear the new insignia for a while. And then he asked you what else Mr. Zupljanin actually did to help. You said that Zupljanin was speaking in a reconciliatory tone and trying, in your view, to calm the situation down. Don't you think that given the circumstances of that meeting at that time, April 9th, 1992, and the number of Muslims in the police department, coming to that meeting with that new insignia might make some of the non-Serbs, the Muslims, in the Prijedor SJB feel uneasy about the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this issue, I wouldn't be able to tell you, even as I think about it on my own without your question. I don't know how millions of people feel in their own state where they wear their own insignia and where is that boundary between this feeling of bearing one's own insignia or somebody else's? Since I have no personal experience, it is very difficult to proffer any opinion. I recall His Honour's question. I did think about it later. What was the merit of Mr. Zupljanin? Well, I could sum it up in the following. What is the merit of head of fire brigade once that fire brigade was able to save only three houses from burning down? That's how I view the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand what you're saying and I'm, you know, I'm glad I didn't have to live through what you lived through or be in that place at that time. I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you were lucky in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. But you said you thought about what Mr. Judge Harhoff had asked you. Let me ask the question this way and see if you might have an answer for it. If it had been the other way around. What if it had been Hebib or somebody coming from Sarajevo and telling you all in the Prijedor station that from now on you were going to wear this new insignia with the three lilies or the crescent moon? How do you think the Serbs in Prijedor SJB would have felt about that? Wouldn't they have felt uneasy?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was not an assumption. It was a reality in some other areas because in our region some stayed behind, others left, and that was true for other areas. All of these were lived-through realities. This happened in Prijedor. The situation that happened in Zenica was the inverse one as well as in Bihac. Who was right? That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, my question, though, wasn't about who was right or wrong. It was about how a particular group felt.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How they felt?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I was asking you originally how do you think the Muslim police in Prijedor felt when Mr. Zupljanin came and was proposing that they wear this new insignia. And you said you couldn't know that, you didn't know how they felt. So I gave you sort of the reverse question and said how would you and the other Serbs in the Prijedor SJB feel if it had been --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... You wouldn't have felt uncomfortable if somebody tried to get you on April 9th to start wearing an insignia with the Bosnian emblem?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is at stake is the feelings of every single individual. You remember when I spoke of that meeting where that dispatch was received? I told you that there was several hundred people present there and that only few of them said that they were opposed to the idea. Everybody else was in favour of us joining Sarajevo. Why? Well, the motivation was the salary. Well, and then if you come up with this idea of the insignia coupled with secure money, some people will fall for it. There is no point in me giving you a universal answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll talk about the 29th meeting and I wasn't trying to tie the insignia to salary because I understand salary is a different motivation that may motivate everybody whatever their ethnicity is. Let me continue on with one more question about the 9th of April and then we'll go to a different topic. One of the last things you said about the meeting was that you were concerned that "... they had the opportunity to decide that fate of ours, and in that context I was bit concerned by the fact that these two took up such a hard line where they wouldn't desist an inch." I just want to be clear. I understood there you were talking about Hasan Talundzic and Fikret Kadiric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fikret.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was his last name, Kadiric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kadiric, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's who you meant who were taking a hard line and not --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you were asked about something you said earlier where you said your higher-ups did not want a war and you were asked who you meant by your higher-ups. And you said: "My minister, my president of the country, or my prime minister." Can you tell me who you meant in that context. Who was your minister? Who was your president of the country? Who was your prime minister when you said that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. But I really have to explain that. Why? For a long time, relatively long time until that time, I was in the police so I had learned to be thinking in a police way. So for me it was only Mr. Zupljanin there. As for everything else, I wasn't interested in the name of the minister or the name of the president of the state, but I know that their will was being carried out through him. This is what I believe. So you cannot have the minister, for example, asking for one thing and then the chief of the centre to come and to be saying something else. No name was put forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, but this was your answer and you said --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who were you referring to by name? Who was your president of your country? Who was your minister --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I not clear? Am I not clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my police system of thought there are no names, there is just him and then above him those up there. There are no names. Those up there. And as they say that what he says is the will of those --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... but the reason I -- but the reason I --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I asked the question and asked for names as to who you're referring to is that on the 6th of April Bosnia had been internationally recognised by European Union and United States. So in essence in that area there were arguably two presidents of the country and two ministers because there was Minister Mico Stanisic of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and there was Minister Delimustafic of the other MUP. And there was President Karadzic of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and there was President Delimustafic -- Izetbegovic. So who were you referring to when you said "my minister" and "my president"? By name which ones were you talking about in that answer on April 9th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, this is a political question and the proof that I don't know politics and that I'm not interested in that is that for three years I don't have a television and I don't even have a mobile telephone. In my service I'm just listening to my superior, to my chief of the centre -- not the centre, actually, the chief of the station of course who's my immediate superior. And then if it should come in -- I mean, if the chief of the centre would come as he would from time to time and says something, I do not doubt that what he says is in accordance with the official state policy and I don't think that it is. I think whatever he says would be in line with that. I don't even know the dates when and who was there. So what I'm saying is actually true. You can check that right now I don't have a TV in my house, meaning that I don't listen to any news. Perhaps I'm not like any other regular man, but that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe you that you don't have a TV in your house. I won't pursue that any further. Let me show you another exhibit, this is tab 34. It's 65 ter number 20063. With the usher's assistance I'll hand you a hard copy. I think you mentioned before after the take-over on the 30th of April that people were required to sign a solemn declaration in the Prijedor police station. Is that right? Now that you were working in this new police station of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia, later called the Republika Srpska, everybody was required to do a new solemn declaration, right, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you sign one yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What? You mean solemn declaration like this? Well, I don't recall that I did, but I think that I had to have signed it because somewhere it must state that I did. I did not sign it that morning when those who came to work that morning signed it. I wasn't there. Later I had to have signed it. I think that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know the person named on this document, Zivko Andzic, did he work in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know. There were many reserve policemen who stayed after that. I don't know this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you don't -- do you remember, did you read the declaration that you signed or did you just sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, perhaps I read it out of curiosity -- well, as but -- if it were important to me or not, I don't know. When everyone signed it, I signed it too. Perhaps I read it. I don't remember if I did or not. Perhaps I was rushing off somewhere, so I just signed and didn't read it. I don't remember. Probably somebody was making lists to make sure that each of the employees did sign it and I don't believe that my name next to that was blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember signing a similar declaration when you first joined the police back in 1980?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was almost identical to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But not exactly identical; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it wasn't in the Cyrillic script, but the sense of it was -- it wasn't the same gazette, it was a different gazette, and so on and so forth. But the sense of it you could say was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people in Prijedor declined to sign the new solemn declaration? Was it very many?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said -- I mean, I said that yesterday more or less. A smaller number stayed. Perhaps those who were working in the offices, four or five. As for the police working on the ground, I don't know. I don't know how many of them stayed. I didn't get that information through my work and there's no need for me to go around asking who did. I don't have the right or the need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know of any Serbs in Prijedor SJB who didn't sign the declaration and stopped working after 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were those who didn't come to work and then after a day or two they did come. I guess they were afraid that there would be shooting so they ran away, but then when they saw that there would be no shooting they came back, they came back for the salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you another document. This is at tab 57. I'll give you a hard copy of that one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we leave this document we could perhaps try and clarify with Mr. Jankovic just how he understood the letter-head of this solemn declaration. Because, Mr. Jankovic, when you said that the gist of the declaration that we have in front of us was the same as the one that you had signed when you first entered the MUP forces back in the 1980s, the difference would seem to me to be the very first word of the letter-head of this declaration that we have in front of us. And so my question to you, Mr. Jankovic, is: Are you able to tell us whether any of those who refused to sign the solemn declaration, regardless of their ethnicity, refused because of the allegiance that you were now supposed to pledge towards the Serbian Republic of BiH? Was that the reason why some members of the MUP refused to sign, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, that morning when they were supposed to sign when they came to work, there was no form. There was just a kind of list. The form appeared later. I think that that morning the form wasn't the way it is now and these people signed some paper, a list of names. As for this, who made it, distributed it, signed it, I don't remember that, and the date is the 5th of May, so five days later. Somebody made that later, but it was being signed already in the morning, that first morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me put my question to you in a different way then. Were you aware when you signed this declaration on that morning that you were now pledging allegiance to the RS? Was that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me repeat this right away. I said that that morning when they were signing that list, I didn't come there because I was away on some other tasks and I came to the station later. And I probably signed it then, maybe not the list. As for this, the question whether I was aware -- well, you know what it's like when the mass sets off. If everybody's going to die, I'm going to do that as well. There's no question, if everybody signed, I'm going to sign it too. But then as a result of that, there are other questions that follow. If I don't sign, what am I going to do, how am I going to manage? What am I going to do? I have two children, an apartment, I'm living in a certain environment. Roughly speaking, there are two groups in the population, there's the Serb side, the Muslim side. Which side am I going to join? I mean, it's not a wrong question. I didn't declare myself as a Serb or a Muslim myself, I mean the nature would pull me one way, but as for the political and legal aspects of that question -- well, I never thought about that. I don't know about the meaning of that now. I mean, I was as sincere as I can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jankovic, it must have occurred to you by the time you signed this declaration that this would have an impact because you were now choosing side, weren't you? And so since you probably made those considerations yourself, I would imagine that you also considered the reasons why some of the colleagues of yours did not sign that declaration, meaning that they too had chosen a side but that they had chosen the other side by refusing to sign. Didn't this occur to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the events were fast and furious then, so I didn't even have time to think. Perhaps now that we're free and we can think about and ponder things. At the time what my thing was was to organise the communications and -- well, it was I can't say general chaos, but it was. At that first initial moment I didn't even think of a yes or a no, but there was no paper like this either. I said that I do not recall this paper. I have a feeling I'm seeing it for the first time, but I believe I probably am not seeing it for the first time, that it exists, that I did sign it. When I look at the date I think I could not have gone without signing it then. So I simply went with the majority, and for me that was the only possible thing to do at the time and sufficient. As for how I would fare in the end, would I die? Well, I would fare just like the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure we can get any further here. Mr. Hannis, back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you another exhibit now. This is P790. It's tab 57. And if I can trade this one for that one. This is dated the 29th of May, 1992, and it's a list of Prijedor police station employees who signed the solemn declaration and of those who did not. I think on the back you'll see it has the name of Dusan Jankovic as the station commander. Can you have a look at the back page. Can you have a look at the back page, and you see Dusan Jankovic's name as the commander, but it looks like somebody else has signed for him on the bottom right at the back page. Do you find it. Is that Kecan?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looks like that. I cannot say but it does look like Kecan as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was Kecan?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You see, we've got I think 72 names of people who signed it and 41 names who did not. Based on your own personal knowledge do you have any reason to disagree with this list as far as those who signed and apparently stayed on working there and those who didn't sign and therefore didn't continue to work in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this list once when the gentleman from the OTP spoke with me earlier and I'm seeing it now, and since this is a list of workers of the SN -- the police station of Prijedor, this is above my organisational unit, I know the name -- the people by name. I don't know anything else, what -- I mean anything else I would say would be superfluous. What would I have to say about somebody else's organisational unit, the one with this commander? At that time I had five or six workers. I don't know if I had to write about anybody then. I didn't see this list before, never really thought about it. I don't have much thoughts about it now either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but I guess the point is you must have known several of these people because they worked as police in Prijedor at the time you were working there and you'd been in the police since 1980. Didn't you know most of these people by name?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not most of them. But, for example, I know Vahid Rizvanovic, Mevlida Boric, I recall her a little bit. Ermin Alagic. There were stations that were outside of Prijedor. I said -- I mentioned these two, but then also in Prijedor the police has their post on the street so I know that it's a policeman. When I encounter him I greet him, but I will say which ones I know. Are you saying those who didn't sign? Who are you thinking of exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, of the names you know, is there anybody who is not correctly listed if you understand what I mean. Do you see anybody you know who is listed as having signed who did not continue to work or do you see anybody who is listed as having not signed who did continue to work? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, I don't know. Why don't I know? I don't know because I don't know about this action by the commander who signed and who did not. As I say, I'm seeing this list for the first time. I saw it from your associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But what I'm saying is of the people you know do you see somebody on the list who did not sign who was still working after this date, 29 May, of those 41? Any of those 41 who did not sign who you personally know, did you see any of them still working for the police after 29 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual act of signing was so significant for me that I don't know whether I signed it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the rest of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking if you could repeat the rest of your sentence. They didn't catch it. Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be briefer and more slow, meaning the act of signing this, as far as I'm concerned, was so significant that I don't even know if I signed it or not. I think that I did but I'm not sure. Perhaps I did not. And because of that fact how can I know in the police station whether such and such a person signed it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, that's not my question. There's a list of people who Kecan or Dusan Jankovic are indicating did not sign. The practical effect at that time, according to directions from Mr. Zupljanin in Banja Luka was that those who didn't sign couldn't continue to work in the police. Now, do you know any names on the list of 41 on that document who did not sign? Do you recognise any of those names among the 41; and if so, tell me which ones?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to be as specific as possible again. The commander who was here, Jankovic Dusan, he made that list and then he went to his superior and handed it over. For example, I have nothing to do with that. For example, I meet Jankovic, Dusan, I know him, I don't ask him Dusan, did you sign it or not. You don't ask people things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't need to talk to him or know him to answer my question. Let's take it one step at a time. First of all, the names on the right, 1 through 41, do you know any of those people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and if so, tell me the number and name of the ones you do know or did know in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember the name. I don't know where she was working, Mevlida Boric; Ermin Alagic, I don't know; Edin Mrkalj, policeman, I forgot his face, I don't know anything more; Senad Mujkanovic, I don't even remember the name; Maid Bahonjic, never heard of him; Mirsad Alic, I don't know about him --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And give me the number along with the name. It will make it easier for all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it appears to me this is going to take a little while so perhaps we should pick this up tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's an excellent idea, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And perhaps he can keep the document overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am happy to have him do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if I may assist, Mr. Jankovic, as I understand Mr. Hannis's question, it is this: Assuming that the document is accurate in terms of those on the right as having not signed, so in other words you don't have to apply your mind as to how the names got there, how this was prepared, but beginning with the assumption that that's an accurate list of those who did not sign, there apply your mind to Mr. Hannis's question and as we said you can keep the list overnight and then he will resume tomorrow morning. So we take the adjournment and continue at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of October, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
